sections.heading: 01 — Core Principles
sections.intro:
Five patterns recur across this collection often enough to treat as load-bearing, even though the
source channel never states them as a single list. Read these first — they're the lens the rest of
this package applies to any specific emergency.

---

subsections.body:
The channel's own stated ranking puts recognition and calling for help ahead of hands-on skill:
"the most important first aid skill... is recognizing when something is seriously wrong, and
calling the emergency medical services early." Every emergency covered in this collection repeats
some version of the same instruction — call before, or while, treating, not after — and several
notes name specific numeric escalation triggers rather than leaving "call for help" as vague advice
(a seizure lasting over five minutes, bleeding that hasn't stopped after 30 minutes, a burn larger
than about 1% of body surface). Where a specific trigger exists, it's worth remembering as a
concrete threshold, not just a general sense that "this seems bad."
subsections.heading: 1. Recognizing and escalating early matters more than any single technique

subsections.body:
Across recovery position, choking, seizures, and CPR, the recurring physical objective is keeping
an airway open or clear, not immobilizing the person. The recovery position exists specifically so
vomit or blood can drain rather than block the airway. Seizure first aid is explicit that
restraining someone is actively wrong — protect them from injury, don't hold them down. Choking
response (back slaps, thrusts) exists to physically clear an obstruction rather than to keep the
person still.
subsections.heading: 2. Protect the airway and don't restrain — most techniques serve one of those two goals

subsections.body:
The same underlying goal — an open airway, a cleared obstruction — is achieved differently for an
adult, a child, and an infant, because infant anatomy behaves oppositely to adult anatomy in at
least one specific way: tilting an infant's head back (which opens an adult's airway) closes an
infant's. This collection's infant-specific notes exist because applying the adult technique
unmodified would be actively counterproductive, not just less optimal.
subsections.heading: 3. Technique is adapted by age and anatomy, not swapped for a different goal

subsections.body:
Several notes name a "don't" that isn't about the immediate injury but about not creating a second
problem: don't wrap a burn tightly (it will need to be removed, causing more damage, and tight
cling film loses its "doesn't stick" benefit); don't put anything in a seizing person's mouth;
don't layer a fresh dressing over a soaked one; don't apply creams, sprays, or medication a first
aider isn't positioned to safely administer. The shared theme is that the first aider's job is
narrower than it might feel in the moment — stabilize and enable further care, don't try to fully
resolve the underlying problem.
subsections.heading: 4. Don't do things that make monitoring or later treatment harder

subsections.body:
This collection includes at least one explicit warning against over-generalizing (seizures: "never
think there's a normal seizure") and at least one place where the same video gives two slightly
different numbers for the same fact within minutes of each other (infant breathing rate). Those
aren't treated as errors to silently correct — they're preserved as-stated, because a first aider
relying on this material should know where the source itself is uncertain or approximate, rather
than being handed false precision.
subsections.heading: 5. When a source hedges, that hedge is part of the information

sections.heading: 02 — Emergency Quick Reference
sections.intro:
A by-emergency lookup pulling together every procedure this collection covers. This is a summary
for fast orientation — the individual notes carry the full detail, direct quotation, and
timestamps this file leaves out. **This collection is not a substitute for emergency medical
services or first-aid certification training.** When in doubt, or for anything not covered here,
call emergency services.

---

subsections.body:
1. Check the area for danger, check for a response, shout for help / call emergency services.
2. Open the airway (head-tilt chin-lift for an adult or child — **not** for an infant, see below).
3. Look, listen, feel for normal breathing for 10 seconds.
4. If breathing normally, do a head-to-toe secondary survey for injury.
5. If no injury found, place in the **recovery position**: link the far hand under the near cheek,
   bend the near knee, roll toward you using the knee, keep the knee at 90° so they stay on their
   side, re-open the airway.
6. If a fracture prevents the recovery position, keep them on their back and hold the airway open
   manually instead.
subsections.heading: Unresponsive but breathing (adult)

subsections.body:
Same sequence, with two changes: keep the airway **neutral** (not tilted either direction — tilting
either way closes an infant's airway), and use a cradle hold instead of a floor roll: supporting
the jaw to keep the airway neutral, head slightly lower than the bottom so vomit drains away.
subsections.heading: Unresponsive but breathing (infant, 0–1)

subsections.body:
- **Partial obstruction** (coughing, making noise): encourage coughing, stay calm, don't intervene
  physically.
- **Complete obstruction** (silent, can't breathe): call emergency services, then alternate up to 5
  back slaps (heel of hand, between shoulder blades) with up to 5 abdominal thrusts (thumb-in-fist
  under the ribcage, above the belly), repeating until it clears or they become unconscious. If
  unconscious: check breathing, ensure ambulance is called, begin CPR.
subsections.heading: Choking — adult or child

subsections.body:
Same back-slap/thrust alternation, but thrusts go **in line with the nipples** (a slower, harder
push than a CPR compression, not the same motion) rather than in the abdomen, and the airway is
kept neutral throughout.
subsections.heading: Choking — infant (0–1)

subsections.body:
If unresponsive and not breathing normally: call emergency services immediately, start CPR
immediately (**30 compressions : 2 breaths**), get a defibrillator (AED) if one is nearby. If found
collapsed on a bed, current guidance is to start CPR **on the bed** rather than delaying to move
them to the floor — remove pillows, push slightly deeper to compensate for the soft mattress. With
helpers present, continue CPR non-stop while a helper retrieves the AED; apply it the moment it
arrives, without delay. **Adult AED pad placement:** one pad under the right clavicle, one under
the left armpit, a hand's width apart, on dry bare skin. An AED cannot shock unless it's needed —
applying one cannot itself cause harm.
subsections.heading: CPR / cardiac arrest — adult

subsections.body:
Check breathing for up to 10 seconds; if not breathing, give 5 rescue breaths, then compressions
with **one hand** to **one-third body depth**, in a **15 compressions : 2 breaths** cycle, until an
AED arrives. AED: pediatric pads if available, otherwise adult pads (placement: one to the left of
the chest midline, one directly opposite on the back). Follow the shock-advised/no-shock-advised
prompt; resume CPR after any shock.
subsections.heading: CPR / cardiac arrest — child

subsections.body:
| | Heart attack | Cardiac arrest |
|---|---|---|
| What's happening | Circulation problem (blocked artery) | Electrical problem (heart stops pumping) |
| Consciousness | Usually conscious, breathing, talking | Unresponsive |
| Signs | Chest pain, pain in arm/jaw, sweaty, feels sick | Not breathing normally |
| Do | Sit down, keep calm, call EMS, give their own prescribed medication | Call EMS, start CPR now, get an AED |
subsections.heading: Heart attack vs. cardiac arrest — telling them apart

subsections.body:
Recognize with **FAST**: **F**ace (fallen on one side, smile not symmetrical), **A**rms (can't
raise both/keep them level), **S**peech (slurred, trouble speaking), **T**ime (call emergency
services immediately if any of these are present — faster treatment saves more of the brain). Once
called: help them into the recovery position on their affected side, keep warm and calm, keep
onlookers away. A temporary version (a TIA/"mini stroke") still needs emergency treatment even if
symptoms resolve. Don't let a plausible mimic (a previous injury, alcohol/drugs, a diabetic hypo)
talk you out of calling — when in doubt, call.
subsections.heading: Stroke

subsections.body:
Signs: itchy skin or raised rash, swollen eyes/lips/hands/feet, lightheadedness, wheezing/breathing
difficulty, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, collapse. Call emergency services immediately, then
use the person's own auto-injector pen (EpiPen or Jext): remove the cap (needle comes from the
opposite end), press firmly against the outer thigh through clothing until it clicks, **hold for
10 seconds** (simplifies the EpiPen's official 3s vs. Jext's 10s), then massage the site. A second
dose can be given after 5 minutes if breathing difficulty continues — always carry two pens.
subsections.heading: Anaphylaxis / severe allergic reaction

subsections.body:
Call emergency services immediately. Treat the underlying blood/fluid loss directly (bandage and
pressure for bleeding). Lay the person down, raise their legs, keep them warm. **Give nothing to
eat or drink** (risk of vomiting under anesthesia, and digestion diverts blood from the heart,
lungs, and brain that need it most). Signs: pale/cold/clammy skin, anxiety progressing toward
unresponsiveness, weak/fatigued limbs, dizziness, blurred vision, nausea, rapid shallow breathing
("air hunger"). Other shock types exist (cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive — including septic
and anaphylactic) but aren't detailed in this collection beyond the hypovolemic case.
subsections.heading: Shock (hypovolemic — blood/fluid loss)

subsections.body:
Immobilize, don't move. A finger: strap to a neighboring finger. An arm at the side: keep still,
sling if needed. A suspected broken leg, pelvis, or skull: **do not move them at all** — call an
ambulance. Two sling options for arm injuries: a **support sling** (sprained wrist, broken humerus
or forearm — tied at the side of the neck, not behind it) or an **elevation sling** (broken
clavicle or dislocated shoulder — bandage over the top of the arm, tied behind the back). Keep the
casualty warm while waiting for help.
subsections.heading: Fracture

subsections.body:
If uncertain whether someone is hyper- or hypoglycemic and can't test their blood sugar: **give
sugar anyway** (full-fat Coke, jam, jelly babies, glucose gel/tablets) and call emergency services —
sugar won't harm a hyperglycemic person, but could save someone who's hypoglycemic and
deteriorating fast. Hyperglycemic signs (slower onset): thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath.
Hypoglycemic signs (fast onset): dizziness, aggression, irritability, sweating. A first aider should
not perform a blood-sugar test on someone else unless specifically trained/authorized to.
subsections.heading: Diabetic emergency

subsections.body:
**Heat exhaustion** (38°C+, hot/sweaty/distressed): move to shade/cool environment, sips of water,
keep calm. **Heat stroke** (~40°C, thermostat failure — key sign: sweating has *stopped*, skin is
dry): medical emergency — remove from heat source, call emergency services, cool actively while
waiting, in order of preference: whole-body cold-water immersion (1–26°C) → cold shower/hose → ice
packs at neck/armpits/groin wrapped in a towel. A related risk in children: a fever-driven
**febrile convulsion**, treated the same as any seizure (protect, don't restrain) while also
working to lower their temperature.
subsections.heading: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke

subsections.body:
Stay calm. Protect from injury (clear the area, cushion the head — never hold it). **Never
restrain. Never put anything in the mouth. Don't move them unless they're in danger. Don't try to
bring them around. Don't give food or drink until fully recovered.** Time the seizure. Once it
ends: check breathing, place in recovery position, stay with them until fully conscious. Call an
ambulance if: it's a first seizure or history is unknown, it lasts over 5 minutes, a second seizure
follows without regaining consciousness in between, or breathing stops (begin CPR).
subsections.heading: Seizure

subsections.body:
Clean if there's time — but if bleeding is heavy, skip cleaning and go straight to pressure (delay
risks hypovolemic shock). Pressure, then a dressing sized to the wound. If blood soaks through,
remove and re-press rather than layering a new dressing on top. **Palm wound across the hand:**
pack with gauze, have them make a fist (closes that orientation of wound — don't do this for a
wound running up-and-down the palm). **Head wound:** wrap at the base of the skull, not higher.
subsections.heading: Bleeding / cuts

subsections.body:
Lean **forward**, not back (tilting back sends blood down the throat). Pinch the soft part of the
nose (below the bony bridge) with firm, continuous pressure for 10 minutes without checking. Repeat
for another 10 if still bleeding. Seek medical help if it hasn't stopped after 30 minutes, is
heavy, or followed a head injury.
subsections.heading: Nosebleed

subsections.body:
Cool under running water for **at least 20 minutes**, regardless of cause (fire, hot surfaces —
including hot sand — sun, chemicals, electricity). If skin has been removed, protect afterward with
cling film loosely layered (not tight) over the area. **Never**: creams, ointments, ice, butter,
touching the burn, bursting a blister, or removing stuck clothing. Seek medical help for a burn on
a child/baby, one larger than about 1% of body surface (roughly a palm), a full-thickness burn, one
that goes all the way around a limb, or any burn on the head, hands, feet, or genitals.
subsections.heading: Burns

subsections.body:
**Reach, throw, don't go.** Don't enter the water after someone struggling — call emergency
services (coast guard if coastal, fire rescue if inland), tell them to float (head back, ears in
water, relax), then reach with something (towel, branch, rope) or throw something buoyant, staying
low and keeping your weight back. If you fall in yourself: float, don't fight the cold-water-shock
urge to thrash.
subsections.heading: Drowning / water rescue

subsections.body:
Base contents on an actual needs assessment for the setting, not a fixed list (BS 8599 is a UK
reference standard, not a legal requirement). Typical contents: disposable ice packs; sterile
dressings in small/medium/large; scissors; micropore tape; triangular bandages; hypoallergenic
plasters; cleaning wipes; latex-free gloves and (at least two, for two helpers) face shields; foil
blankets (for keeping an *already-warm* casualty warm, not for warming a cold one); general PPE.
Consider adding: safety pins, sterile water/saline, tweezers, a guidance leaflet, a pocket mask,
compression bandages. **Never include** "potions, lotions, and sprays" — painkillers, medicated
creams, or sprays a first aider isn't qualified to administer.
subsections.heading: Building a first aid kit

sections.heading: 07 — Plain English Glossary
sections.intro:
Every technical term introduced across this knowledge package, defined the way the source material
defines it. Terms are alphabetical.

---

subsections.body:
**AED** — an automated external defibrillator, used interchangeably with "defibrillator" in the
source material: the device that analyzes heart rhythm and advises whether a shock is needed.
subsections.heading: A

subsections.body:
**Cold water shock** — the sudden loss of the ability to control breathing on entering cold water.
Fighting the sensation, rather than floating through it, is what the source material describes as
the actual mechanism of drowning.
subsections.heading: C

- **Emergencies:** a general allergic reaction (sneezing, wheezing, coughing, skin rash), anaphylaxis — a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction affecting the respiratory system
- **Procedures:** call emergency medical services immediately if anaphylaxis is suspected, then retrieve the person's auto-injector pen, have them sit in a comfortable position (a "W" position is suggested, but comfort takes priority), remove the cap (from the opposite end to where the needle emerges), press the injector firmly against the outer thigh through clothing (no need to undress the area) until it clicks, hold in place, then gently massage the site, a second dose can be given after 5 minutes if the person is still struggling to breathe — stated reasons a second pen may be needed: a missed injection, an accidental self-injection by the helper, or the pen's dose simply not being enough while waiting for the ambulance, a person with a known severe allergy should always carry two auto-injector pens; check they have both, and know where they are, if responsible for someone with this condition
- **Important concepts:** an allergen defined as any substance triggering an allergic reaction, with named common examples: pollen, house dust mites, mold, pets, nuts, fruits, latex, dairy, the specific hold-time discrepancy between EpiPen (3 seconds) and Jext (10 seconds) auto injectors — the source's stated workaround is to just hold every pen for 10 seconds regardless, to remove the need to remember which

- **Main subjects:** animal bites (dogs/cats), hairy caterpillar (oak processionary moth) toxin exposure, and safe tick removal with Lyme disease awareness
- **Emergencies:** an animal bite (dog or cat) causing bleeding, tears, bruising, or broken bones, hairy caterpillar (oak processionary moth) hair exposure — itchy rash, and rarely eye/throat irritation or breathing problems, a tick bite, with the risk of Lyme disease
- **Procedures:** for an animal bite: first ensure the scene is safe (e.g. the biting animal is removed/ controlled), then treat as any other bleed — clean the wound, apply pressure, seek medical help if needed, for hairy caterpillar hair exposure: do not rub the area; remove the hairs with tweezers, or rinse under running water and air-dry (not rub dry), then lift hairs out with sticky tape; monitor breathing, for a tick: remove promptly and carefully with a tick remover (placed under the tick, twisted 360°) or fine tweezers, ensuring the head comes out with the body; never burn it, cover it in Vaseline, or spin it to make it "dizzy," since this can cause the tick to regurgitate its contents into the wound and increase disease risk, keep a removed tick in a sealed bag or container in the freezer in case it needs testing for Lyme disease later, and to show medical professionals the whole tick (including the head) was removed, prevention for ticks: wear long trousers and socks in woodland/long grass, and check yourself, clothing, and pets afterward
- **Important concepts:** the oak processionary moth caterpillar named specifically as the toxic hairy caterpillar of concern, recognizable by nesting in oak trees and moving in a "procession" line, Lyme disease described as a serious illness with flu-like symptoms, lethargy, and body aches, with about 50% of cases developing a "bullseye" rash, and — if not promptly treated — potential for paralysis, arthritis, or meningitis

- **Main subjects:** preparing a child with an ongoing medical condition for school — individual healthcare plans, carrying and administering their own medication, and UK school policy on spare emergency medication
- **Emergencies:** none recorded
- **Procedures:** encourage a child to carry and, where appropriate, self-administer their own emergency medication (inhaler, auto-injector pen) at school rather than having it locked away and inaccessible, for a child with a complex or ongoing medical condition (e.g. asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, severe allergies): request an Individual Healthcare Plan (IHP) from the school specifying what help the school will provide and what staff can administer in an emergency, for routine short-term medication (e.g. antibiotics): schedule doses around the school day where possible (morning, after school, bedtime) to avoid needing to bring medication in at all; if it must be brought in, only prescription medication in its original packaging, with written parental consent, and only the smallest amount needed for that day, staff administering or supervising medication in the UK do so voluntarily — the source states teachers are not legally required to give or supervise medication
- **Important concepts:** UK policy context named: the Children and Families Act (introduced September 2014) requiring schools to support pupils with medical needs; schools permitted to hold a spare blue reliever inhaler since 2014, and a spare adrenaline auto-injector pen (e.g. EpiPen) since October 2017 — both described as optional for a school to stock, not compulsory, and not a substitute for the child's own medication, a stated statistic that half of adults with mental health issues report their first symptoms before age 14, used to frame the importance of watching for emotional-health signs alongside physical medical needs

- **Main subjects:** hazards from UK coastal sea life — sharp shells/barnacles, crabs, jellyfish stings, and weever fish stings — with a specific myth correction about jellyfish sting treatment
- **Emergencies:** a jellyfish sting, ranging from a painful mark to (rarely) a severe, life-threatening reaction, a weever fish sting, from standing on one buried in sand
- **Procedures:** wear shoes on rocks and walk slowly into the water to avoid cuts from barnacles/shells and crab pinches, for a jellyfish sting: remove any stuck tentacles with a flat object (e.g. a credit card), never fingers, and without rubbing (which can trigger more venom release); rinse with seawater, not fresh water; then soak the area in water as hot as tolerable for at least 30 minutes (or use hot flannels/towels if soaking isn't possible), do not urinate on a jellyfish sting — explicitly stated to potentially worsen it, the same way fresh water does, by releasing more venom from unfired stingers, for a weever fish sting: remove the embedded dorsal-fin spines from the foot, then immerse the foot in water at 40°C (104°F) or higher for at least 30 minutes, seek medical help or a lifeguard immediately if uncomfortable performing self-treatment, or if in doubt about any marine sting or bite
- **Important concepts:** the shared mechanism behind two counter-intuitive instructions: both urinating on a jellyfish sting and rinsing it with fresh water are stated to activate unfired stingers and release additional venom, rather than providing relief

- **Main subjects:** diabetes as a condition (types 1 and 2), and the first-aid distinction and treatment between a hyperglycemic and a hypoglycemic emergency
- **Emergencies:** a hyperglycemic episode — high blood sugar, slower onset, a hypoglycemic episode ("a hypo") — low blood sugar, fast onset, more urgent to treat
- **Procedures:** a first aider should not perform a blood-sugar test (pin-prick or sensor) on someone else unless specifically trained and authorized to (e.g. as a childminder or nursery worker with a care plan) — encourage the person to test themselves instead, for a hyperglycemic episode: give the person their own prescribed medication (tablets or insulin) to bring sugar levels down, for a hypoglycemic episode: give sugar immediately (a full-fat Coke, jam, jelly babies, glucose gel, or tablets) to raise blood sugar quickly, since a hypo deteriorates fast without correction, if blood sugar can't be tested and the signs are ambiguous, the source's stated rule is to give sugar anyway and call emergency medical services, on the reasoning that sugar will not harm a hyperglycemic person but could save a hypoglycemic one
- **Important concepts:** type 1 diabetes (no insulin production, typically inherited) versus type 2 (insufficient insulin, often linked to being overweight, more common) as the source's basic split, a normal blood-sugar reading stated as 4 to 7; above 7 as hyperglycemic, below 4 as hypoglycemic, hyperglycemic signs (thirst, frequent urination, fruity-smelling breath, slower onset) versus hypoglycemic signs (dizziness, aggression, irritability, sweating, fast onset) as the source's distinguishing pattern, with an explicit caveat that a blood-sugar reading is the only way to know for certain

- **Main subjects:** the drowning-specific CPR sequence (adapted because drowning is a respiratory, not cardiac, event), plus dry drowning and secondary/delayed drowning as distinct, rare complications
- **Emergencies:** an unconscious adult recovered from water, not breathing, dry drowning — a child inhales water that triggers a vocal-cord spasm, preventing air from entering the lungs, without water actually entering the lungs, secondary/delayed drowning — inhaled water causes lung inflammation that can present hours to days (up to 72 hours) after the initial water exposure
- **Procedures:** only enter water to help if it's safe to do so; shout for help first, once the person is on dry land, open the airway and check breathing for 10 seconds as usual, if not breathing: open the airway, pinch the nose, and give 5 rescue breaths first (this may be enough on its own) — if not, begin 30 compressions to 2 breaths and continue for one minute, if alone and the person hasn't recovered after one minute of CPR, leave to call emergency services, then resume care — this differs from an on-land collapse, where the ambulance is called immediately, before starting CPR, if breathing resumes, place in the recovery position and keep warm, seek medical help immediately for any suspected dry or secondary drowning, even if the person seems to recover initially
- **Important concepts:** the key distinction driving the different CPR sequence: a drowning collapse is treated as a respiratory problem (lack of oxygen) rather than a cardiac one, similar in mechanism to why an infant or child might stop breathing, whereas a collapse on dry land is treated as more likely cardiac, both dry and secondary drowning are explicitly stated to be "extremely, extremely rare"

- **Main subjects:** how electrical injury happens and why it can be dangerous to a rescuer, and the scene-safety first, treat-second approach to electrocution
- **Emergencies:** electrocution from mains electricity, high-voltage cables, or other electrical sources
- **Procedures:** ensure the scene is safe before approaching — assume the patient may still be "live" if in contact with the electrical source, and do not touch them if there is any doubt, for a low-voltage source (e.g. household): turn off the power supply at the main, then approach, for a high-voltage source (e.g. overhead cables): stay well back — electricity can arc up to 80 meters through air or ground, more in wet or foggy conditions — and call emergency medical services rather than approaching at all, once safe to approach, check breathing (e.g. by talking to the person as you approach); begin CPR if not breathing, or place in the recovery position if breathing but unconscious, then assess for other injuries including burns, know in advance where the main power supply is, at home or at work, so it can be turned off quickly if needed
- **Important concepts:** as little as 10 milliamps causing muscle contraction strong enough to make a hand close around and be unable to release an electrical source, and as little as 60 milliamps being potentially fatal in wet conditions, electricity causing two separate burn sites (entry and exit points), described as often severe and slow to heal because the damage penetrates deep into the body, the body becoming "the link from live to earth" when a body part contacts or nears a live source, explaining why an electrocuted person can remain dangerous to touch

- **Emergencies:** heart attack — a blocked artery stopping blood reaching the heart muscle, person usually conscious, breathing, and talking, cardiac arrest — the heart stops pumping altogether, person is unresponsive and not breathing normally
- **Procedures:** for a heart attack — sit the person down, keep them calm, call emergency medical services, and give any medication they have been told by their doctor to take, for cardiac arrest — call emergency medical services immediately, start CPR immediately, and get a defibrillator if one is nearby

- **Main subjects:** the body's temperature-regulation "thermostat," and what happens when it fails at either temperature extreme, with a focus on heat exhaustion and heat stroke
- **Emergencies:** heat exhaustion (body temperature at or above 38°C, hot, sweaty, distressed), heat stroke (body temperature around 40°C, thermostat failure, a medical emergency), febrile convulsion in a child, caused by a rapid body-temperature rise
- **Procedures:** for heat exhaustion: move to a cooler/shaded environment, give sips of water, keep calm, for heat stroke: remove from the heat source immediately and call emergency medical services, then actively cool the patient while waiting — in order of preference: whole-body immersion from the neck down in water between 1 and 26°C, then a cold shower or garden hose, then ice in bags wrapped in a towel placed on the neck, armpits, and groin, or wet towels (removing and replacing a wet towel with a dry one once cooled, to avoid overcooling), for a febrile convulsion: treat the same as any seizure (keep safe, never hold down), while also trying to bring the temperature down; call emergency medical services if in doubt
- **Important concepts:** 37°C as the source's stated normal body temperature, with below 35°C as hypothermia, 38°C and above as heat exhaustion, and 40°C as heat stroke, the loss of sweating (dry skin) as the key distinguishing sign that heat exhaustion has progressed to the more dangerous heat stroke, dehydration named as the underlying risk factor across all heat-related problems

- **Emergencies:** an infant (0-1) choking, silent and gasping
- **Procedures:** keep the infant's airway neutral throughout (neither tilted back nor forward, both of which are stated to close a baby's airway), supporting the jawline with one hand, up to five back slaps with the heel of the hand, head lower than the bottom, checking after each one for the blockage to clear, if back slaps don't work, turn the infant over (airway still supported, head still lower than the bottom) and give up to five chest thrusts — two fingers in line with the nipples, described as a slower, harder push than a CPR compression, not a compression itself, repeat the back-slap/chest-thrust cycle, call emergency medical services if the blockage persists, and begin CPR if the infant becomes unresponsive and is not breathing
- **Important concepts:** infant chest thrusts (in line with the nipples) as a distinct technique from adult/child abdominal thrusts, and explicitly distinguished from a CPR compression by speed and force

- **Main subjects:** concussion myths, how to recognize concussion via visible signs and reported symptoms, and the graduated rest-then-return-to-sport timeline recommended by UK sporting governing bodies
- **Emergencies:** suspected concussion following a direct or transmitted-force blow to the head or body
- **Procedures:** if concussion is suspected: "if in doubt, sit them out" — stop the activity immediately, rest completely (physically and mentally), never leave the person alone; keep them with a responsible adult who can monitor for deterioration and knows how to get help, do not let them drive, and discourage alcohol for at least 24 hours, if signs deteriorate, or seizures occur, or a spinal injury/broken limb is suspected: keep them warm, do not move them, and call emergency medical services, return-to-sport timeline: 24–48 hours of full rest (physical and cognitive), then a graduated return-to-play protocol; no sport-specific training for at least 14 days, no competition for at least 21 days — with progression through the protocol only continuing if an activity doesn't more than mildly worsen symptoms
- **Important concepts:** three common concussion myths named and corrected: that a person must be knocked unconscious (in fact this occurs in under 10% of concussions), that a head injury must have occurred (concussion can result from a transmitted or whiplash-type force elsewhere on the body), and that it would show on imaging (concussion cannot be seen on X-ray, CT, or MRI), a sign (something observable) versus a symptom (something the person reports) as the source's basic distinction for recognizing concussion, symptom onset described as sometimes immediate but sometimes delayed up to 72 hours, explicitly given as the reason repeated assessment matters, concussion's effects organized into four areas by the source: physical, cognitive ("mental processing"), mood, and sleep

- **Main subjects:** what a seizure is, the tonic-clonic pattern as a typical (not universal) example, and the first-aid response of protecting rather than restraining the person
- **Emergencies:** a convulsive (tonic-clonic) seizure, a non-convulsive seizure (described as "daydreaming"/absence-type)
- **Procedures:** stay calm, protect the person from injury by moving objects out of the way and cushioning their head (never holding it), never restrain them, and start timing the seizure, look for medical ID (bracelet, necklace, phone, wallet) if the person's history is unknown, carefully, since it may indicate what caused the seizure, once the seizure ends, check breathing, place the person in the recovery position, and keep talking to them until they fully regain consciousness, do not: restrain the person, put anything in their mouth, move them unless they're in danger, try to bring them around forcibly, or give them anything to eat or drink until fully recovered, call an ambulance if: it's a first seizure or the person's history is unknown, the seizure lasts longer than five minutes, a second tonic-clonic seizure follows the first without regaining consciousness in between, the person seems to need urgent medical attention, or they stop breathing (begin CPR in that case)
- **Important concepts:** a convulsive versus non-convulsive seizure as the source's basic split, with epilepsy defined as "a tendency to have recurrent seizures" rather than a single specific cause, the tonic stage (rigid, muscular contraction) followed by the clonic stage (repeated contract-relax convulsions) as the two phases of a typical tonic-clonic seizure, a febrile convulsion in young children, attributed to the brain not yet coping with a rapid rise in body temperature, a possible pre-seizure warning symptom (odd movements, unusual smells or tastes) — the transcript's caption reads "orders," almost certainly a mishearing of the clinical term "auras," but that word is not actually spoken in the available captions — explicitly stated as inconsistent and not present for everyone

- **Main subjects:** the four types of fracture named by the source, the core immobilize-don't-move treatment principle, and two sling techniques demonstrated for arm injuries
- **Emergencies:** a closed fracture (bone broken but not through the skin), an open fracture (bone broken and piercing the skin), a complicated fracture (a break causing a secondary complication, e.g. a punctured lung or trapped nerve), a greenstick/hairline fracture (common in children, whose bones are more flexible)
- **Procedures:** immobilize the injured limb or digit rather than moving it — for a finger, strap it to a neighboring finger; for an arm at the side, keep it still without necessarily needing a sling; for a suspected broken leg while lying down, keep the person still rather than attempting to splint or move them, do not attempt to transport someone with a suspected broken leg, pelvis, femur, or skull fracture yourself — call an ambulance, since moving them "will only make it worse", for less severe arm injuries, once immobilized, the casualty can usually walk to get medical help, or be driven, with next of kin contacted if needed, keep the casualty warm while waiting for help, since a fracture alone is not usually life-threatening but can take time to receive care, support sling: for a suspected sprained wrist, broken humerus, or broken forearm bones — triangular bandage slid between the arm and body, long side vertical, tied at the side of the neck (not behind it), point toward the injured elbow, elevation sling: for a suspected broken clavicle or dislocated shoulder — bandage laid over the top of the arm rather than underneath, tucked from the fingers down to the elbow, gathered and tied behind the back, avoiding pressure directly over the injury
- **Important concepts:** immobilization (not elevation or splinting attempts by an untrained first aider) as the consistent goal across all fracture types, improvising a sling from a jumper or t-shirt as an acceptable substitute when a casualty prefers not to be touched, provided the arm is kept still

- **Main subjects:** the general clean-pressure-dressing approach to treating a bleeding wound, with specific adaptations demonstrated for a palm wound and a head wound
- **Emergencies:** a bleeding wound on a limb, palm, or head, with the risk of hypovolemic shock if bleeding isn't controlled
- **Procedures:** general sequence for any bleed: clean the wound (if time allows), put pressure on it, apply a dressing sized to the wound (small/medium/large), and secure it, checking that a wound bleeding through a dressing gets the dressing replaced rather than layered on top of soaked material, palm wound running across the palm: pack it with gauze and have the casualty make a fist, which is stated to close that orientation of wound (a fist would instead open a wound running up and down the palm, and should not be used for that orientation), head wound: wrap the bandage around the base of the skull rather than higher up, covering top and bottom of the dressing the same way as on a limb

- **Main subjects:** a general burn-treatment rule (cool for 20 minutes, protect with cling film) that applies regardless of cause, plus the SCALD framework for judging burn severity
- **Emergencies:** a burn or scald from any cause — fire, hot surfaces (including hot sand), sun, chemicals, or electricity
- **Procedures:** cool any burn under running water for at least 20 minutes regardless of cause; if no water is available, a gel-based burns dressing is the next-best option, but water is stated as the preferred method, once cooled, protect a burn where skin has been removed by loosely layering cling film over it, not wrapped tightly, so hospital staff can see the wound without removing a dressing, do not put anything other than water on a burn — no creams, ointments, ice, or butter; do not touch the burn or burst a blister; do not remove clothing stuck to the burn, seek medical help for a burn on a child or baby, one larger than about 1% of the body's surface (roughly the size of a palm), a full-thickness burn, one that goes all the way around a limb, or any burn on the head, hands, feet, or genitals
- **Important concepts:** "SCALD" as the source's acronym for judging burn severity: size, cause, age (of the person), location, and depth, the "rule of nines" for estimating burn size as a percentage of total body surface area (one hand is roughly 1 percent; the head 9 percent; front and back of the torso 18 percent each; each leg 18 percent; each arm 9 percent), first-degree/superficial, second-degree/partial-thickness, and third-degree/full-thickness as the three depth categories, with the counterintuitive point that full-thickness burns can hurt less because nerve endings have been destroyed

- **Main subjects:** what happens physically during an asthma attack, the two-inhaler system asthma sufferers carry, and step-by-step technique for using a reliever inhaler with and without a spacer (mouthpiece version) on an adult
- **Emergencies:** an asthma attack — airway muscles tighten, the lining swells, and mucus buildup narrows the airway further, making it hard to breathe out
- **Procedures:** let the person choose their own position (sitting up, a tripod lean over a table, hands behind the head) and encourage opening the chest cavity rather than curling up; loosen tight clothing, always use the casualty's OWN inhaler, never someone else's (cross-contamination risk, and it may be a different medication), without a spacer: press the pump and breathe in, one puff every minute; if not improving after 5 minutes, call emergency medical services and continue one puff per minute until they arrive, with a mouthpiece spacer: shake the inhaler, insert it into the spacer, have the casualty breathe out fully, seal their mouth around the mouthpiece, press one puff into the spacer, have them breathe in slowly (not hard/fast), hold breath ~10 seconds, breathe out slowly; wait 30 seconds before a second dose if needed, never leave an asthma sufferer alone during an attack, and never send them somewhere cold (cold air is a trigger and will tighten an already-tight chest further)
- **Important concepts:** the preventative (brown, typically a steroid, taken morning/night) versus reliever (blue, typically salbutamol, used during an attack) inhaler distinction, a spacer described as delivering a more precise dose directly to the lungs and reducing side effects like oral thrush compared to using a pump inhaler alone

- **Main subjects:** what hyperventilation is (over-breathing that depletes carbon dioxide), and two techniques for breaking the resulting "vicious circle"
- **Emergencies:** hyperventilation — over-breathing, often occurring during a panic attack
- **Procedures:** find a quiet place to sit, release tension in the shoulders and upper body, sit with a straight back, and loosen tight clothing before starting a breathing technique, breath-control technique: breathe in slowly for a count of four, hold for a count of four, breathe out slowly for a count of four, repeating until calm — with an occasional normal breath inserted if needed to avoid dizziness from too many deep breaths in a row, re-breathing technique: cup both hands over the nose and mouth, breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth into the cupped hands, repeated no more than four times, to re-inhale some of the carbon dioxide just exhaled, {'other tips mentioned': 'humming, whistling, or singing can help regulate breathing'}, seek emergency medical advice if unsure whether the presentation is hyperventilation or something else (e.g. a heart attack), since symptoms like chest pain can overlap — never leave the person alone in that uncertainty
- **Important concepts:** hyperventilation explained mechanistically: over-breathing pushes out more carbon dioxide than normal, and the resulting CO2 deficit (not a lack of oxygen) is what produces the symptoms and drives further over-breathing in a self-reinforcing "vicious circle", the brown-paper-bag rebreathing method is explicitly named as no longer taught in first aid, with the source noting medical research on it is described as "divided" on why it works and that it doesn't work for everyone

- **Main subjects:** hypothermia treatment (with the specific warning against rapid rewarming), prevention, and the two related cold-injury conditions frost nip and frostbite
- **Emergencies:** hypothermia — from cold air exposure or cold-water immersion, frost nip — skin freezing, red and white, painful but self-treatable, frostbite — deeper tissue/muscle/blood-vessel freezing, more serious
- **Procedures:** for hypothermia: do not reheat quickly — rapid rewarming can complicate the condition and cause cardiac arrest; if the person is wet, remove wet clothing (water draws heat out 20-25 times faster than air) and dry them by patting gently, then warm gradually, for frost nip: warm the affected area gently yourself (e.g. tucking cold fingertips under the armpits), watching that it doesn't progress to frostbite, for frostbite: do not rub or massage the area (this worsens it); rewarm only slowly, using water no warmer than 40°C, and seek emergency medical guidance since the rewarming process is usually very painful, prevention: carry a change of clothes, towels, and blankets whenever wet conditions or cold water are a possibility, even in summer, and note a standard foil blanket alone is not sufficient to warm someone up, only to help maintain warmth
- **Important concepts:** the specific danger of fast rewarming in hypothermia — named as a cause of cardiac arrest, not just an ineffective approach, water's heat-transfer rate relative to air (stated as 20 to 25 times faster) as the reason wet clothing must be removed even in otherwise mild conditions
subsections.heading: 23. Hypothermia |  Adult First Aid  | EMT First Aid Training

- **Main subjects:** distinguishing a bee sting from a wasp sting (and why it changes treatment), general insect bite/sting symptoms, and recognizing when a bite/sting has become infected or anaphylactic
- **Emergencies:** a bee or wasp sting, a general insect bite (midges, gnats, mosquitoes, fleas, flies, mites, bed bugs), an infected bite/sting, anaphylaxis triggered by a sting
- **Procedures:** for a bee sting (stinger left behind): scrape it out sideways with a flat edge (a credit or business card), never with tweezers or by squeezing at the top — both of those actions push more venom from the embedded sac into the wound, for a wasp sting (no stinger left behind) or a general insect bite: wash with soap and water, apply a cold compress, elevate the area to reduce swelling, and avoid scratching (which risks infection); avoid home remedies like vinegar or bicarbonate of soda, which the source states are "unlikely to help", watch for an allergic reaction after any sting; call emergency services immediately for wheezing, breathing difficulty, facial swelling, feeling or being sick, an increased heart rate, dizziness, or faintness — signs of anaphylaxis, seek medical help if an infection develops (spreading redness, worsening pain or swelling, pus, fever, or swollen glands)
- **Important concepts:** the mechanical distinction between a bee (leaves its stinger embedded) and a wasp (does not) as the reason their first-aid treatment differs, pus described plainly as discharge from an infected bite, with spreading redness/swelling "more likely due to an allergy than to an infection" when it happens quickly

- **Main subjects:** what a panic attack and panic disorder are, their symptoms and typical duration, and the difference between reassuring someone in the moment versus longer-term treatment options
- **Emergencies:** a panic attack — a sudden rush of intense mental and physical symptoms, part of panic disorder when recurrent
- **Procedures:** in the moment: stay calm, remember panic attacks are not life-threatening and won't cause physical harm, stay where you are, and breathe through it — if hyperventilating, use the breathing techniques covered in the companion hyperventilation video, call emergency medical services if there's genuine doubt about whether the presentation is a panic attack or something else, since several symptoms (chest pain, racing heart) overlap with more dangerous conditions, longer-term: encourage seeing a GP to rule out other conditions and discuss treatment — main options named are talking therapy (CBT) and medication (antidepressants, which the source notes can take 2-4 weeks to start working and up to 8 weeks for full effect), self-help measures named: breathing techniques, regular physical exercise, complementary therapies (massage, aromatherapy, yoga, Pilates), and cutting back on sugar, caffeine, alcohol, and smoking, all described as able to worsen attacks
- **Important concepts:** anxiety described as ranging from mild to severe, with panic named as its most severe form, a "cycle of living in fear of fear" — avoiding situations out of fear of triggering another attack, which the source says can itself increase the frequency of attacks, a diagnostic threshold mentioned: regular, unexpected panic attacks followed by at least a month of continuous worry about having further attacks

- **Main subjects:** poisoning by swallowed chemicals/drugs, food poisoning, and plant/fungi poisoning, with a shared core response of identifying the substance and calling emergency services
- **Emergencies:** swallowed poison (household chemicals, drugs — legal or illegal), food poisoning (bacterial or viral contamination, e.g. salmonella or E. coli), plant or fungi poisoning (e.g. foxglove, poisonous berries, death cap mushroom)
- **Procedures:** identify what was taken, how much, and when; reassure the casualty and call emergency medical services with as much detail as possible to help hospital treatment, if the casualty becomes unconscious, open the airway, check breathing, and begin CPR if needed — using a face shield or covering the mouth and blowing through the nose to avoid cross-contamination from residual chemical, do not induce vomiting in a conscious casualty, since vomiting can cause further damage as the substance passes back through the respiratory tract, mouth, and nose, stay calm and non-accusatory, since a scared casualty (especially a child) may not disclose what or how much they took, for food poisoning: rest, hydration (rehydration powders or isotonic drinks), and seeking medical help if needed; report to authorities/employer if relevant (e.g. a shared food source), for plant/fungi poisoning: try to identify the plant or fungus (photograph or bring a sample) to help medical treatment
- **Important concepts:** poison/toxin defined broadly — not only swallowed, but absorbed through skin or eyes, inhaled, or injected, then carried through the bloodstream to organs and tissue, dehydration named as a serious complication of food poisoning, especially for the young, the elderly, or in a hot climate, prevention framed as the primary defense against plant/fungi poisoning — knowing what plants are in one's own garden or house and removing ones dangerous to children or pets

- **Main subjects:** the four medical types of shock (named for completeness), with hypovolemic shock (blood/fluid loss) covered in treatment depth
- **Emergencies:** hypovolemic shock — insufficient circulating blood or fluid, most commonly from hemorrhage or severe vomiting/diarrhea
- **Procedures:** call emergency medical services immediately — shock is treated as a medical emergency, treat the underlying blood or fluid loss directly (e.g. bandage and apply pressure to a bleeding wound), lay the patient down and raise their legs to help circulation reach the brain, lungs, and heart, and keep them warm, give nothing to eat or drink ("nil by mouth"), even if they're thirsty — stated reasons are surgical risk (vomiting under anesthesia) and that digestion would divert blood away from the organs that need it most, keep the patient lying down with legs raised until emergency medical services arrive, even if they start to feel better
- **Important concepts:** the four types of medical shock named by the source: hypovolemic (blood/fluid volume loss), cardiogenic (the heart fails to pump, e.g. from a heart attack or valve problem), obstructive (a blockage restricting blood flow, e.g. of the aorta or venous return), and distributive (abnormal blood distribution to tissue, covering septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock), a stated blood-loss severity scale — shock begins at roughly 20% blood/fluid loss, and death is stated to occur at roughly 40% loss, the body's stated priority order for oxygen delivery during shock: lungs, heart, and brain first, "air hunger" as the source's description of shock-related breathing distress, likened to breathing with a bag over one's head

- **Main subjects:** general snake-bite first aid (identify, immobilize, get to hospital) versus the special pressure-immobilization technique reserved only for known neurotoxic/elapid snake bites, common snake-bite myths and why the source says each one makes things worse
- **Emergencies:** a general snake bite (any species, UK-focused examples given), a bite from a known neurotoxic/elapid snake (non-spitting cobras, mambas, coral snakes, sea snakes, and "actually everything in Australia")
- **Procedures:** general treatment: call emergency medical services and get to hospital fast; stay calm (a raised heart rate speeds venom circulation); keep the bitten limb as still as possible, lying the casualty down, in the recovery position if possible; try to identify the snake's color and pattern; loosen tight clothing and remove jewelry near the bite before swelling starts; draw a mark around the bite, note the time, and record symptoms every 30 minutes, do NOT: approach, catch, or kill the snake; suck or cut venom from the wound; apply ice (constricts vessels, worsens local tissue damage); apply a tourniquet (concentrates venom, worsening tissue destruction); give aspirin or ibuprofen (worsens bleeding); use any commercial "snake bite kit" device, for a confirmed neurotoxic/elapid bite only: apply a broad pressure-immobilization bandage from below the bite upward, over clothing (don't remove clothing, to avoid moving the limb), with pressure similar to a sprained-ankle wrap, then splint the limb; this bandage must not be removed until at hospital with anti-venom ready, since removal causes a rapid venom surge into the bloodstream
- **Important concepts:** "no first aid is often less harmful than bad first aid" as the source's stated governing rule for snake bites specifically, a pressure-immobilization bandage explicitly distinguished from a tourniquet — the source is emphatic the two are not substitutes and a tourniquet is "never ever appropriate for any type of snake bite", identifying the snake's type/pattern is framed as clinically useful for the treating doctor, but not the priority over calling for help

- **Main subjects:** distinguishing a sprain from a strain as soft-tissue injuries, and the shared RICE treatment for both
- **Emergencies:** a sprain — an overstretched ligament (bone-to-bone) at a joint, a strain — a torn or overstretched muscle or tendon (muscle-to-bone)
- **Procedures:** RICE: Rest (stop the activity, get comfortable), Ice (20 minutes maximum, wrapped in a towel if from a freezer rather than a shake-activated cold pack, checking circulation past the injury every 10 minutes), Compression (a crepe bandage, comfortably firm), Elevate (to reduce swelling), move the casualty carefully once initial treatment is done — stand an upper-limb injury up slowly (pain can cause faintness), and get help moving a lower-limb injury since they shouldn't bear weight on it, always advise seeking professional medical help afterward, since a first aider "can't x-ray" and a fracture could be present alongside the soft-tissue injury
- **Important concepts:** a ligament (bone-to-bone) versus a tendon (muscle-to-bone) as the anatomical distinction between what's damaged in a sprain versus a strain — though the source notes a first aider doesn't need to tell the two injuries apart to treat them the same way

- **Main subjects:** what a stroke is (including the two main mechanisms and a TIA/"mini stroke"), the FAST mnemonic for recognizing one, and the first-aid response while waiting for emergency services
- **Emergencies:** a stroke — a sudden interruption of blood supply to part of the brain, a TIA ("mini stroke") — a temporary blockage producing stroke-like symptoms that resolve
- **Procedures:** recognize using FAST: Face (has it fallen on one side, is the smile symmetrical), Arms (can both be raised and held level, or does one drop), Speech (slurred, trouble speaking, drooling), Time (call emergency services immediately if any of these are present), help the person onto the floor and into the recovery position on their affected side, keep them warm (cover with a blanket), calm, and keep onlookers away to protect their dignity and reduce distress, do not give food or drink, and be prepared that bladder or bowel control may be lost
- **Important concepts:** two main stroke mechanisms named: a clot blocking an artery (via thrombosis, embolism, or small-vessel blockage) versus a bleed/hemorrhage from a burst blood vessel in or around the brain, a TIA (transient ischemic attack) as a temporary version of a stroke that still requires emergency treatment, since it signals risk of a more serious stroke later, stroke mimics named explicitly — a previous fall/broken arm, alcohol or drug influence, or a diabetic hypoglycemic episode can all resemble stroke signs, with the source's stated rule being to call emergency services regardless of uncertainty

- **Procedures:** primary survey: check the area for danger (look, listen, smell), check for a response, shout for help / call emergency medical services, open the airway with a head-tilt chin-lift, then look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for 10 seconds, secondary survey: head-to-toe check for lumps/bumps, fluid from the ears (possible spinal sign), medical ID jewelry, lacerations on each arm, sternum/abdomen for signs of internal bleeding, pelvis stability, pocket contents (checked with the back of the hand), and each leg, recovery position: link the far hand under the near cheek, bend the near leg at the knee, roll the person toward you using the knee, keep the knee at 90 degrees so they stay on their side, then re-open the airway, if a broken limb prevents the recovery position, keep the person on their back with the airway held open manually instead, while accepting this ties up the rescuer's hands

- **Main subjects:** what a spinal injury is, how one can happen, and the core "do not move them, support the head" first-aid rule, including the narrow exceptions where moving is necessary
- **Emergencies:** a suspected spinal injury (from a low-level fall, a road accident, a fall from height, or compression such as someone jumping on the back)
- **Procedures:** do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury; support their head and neck, keep them as still as possible, leave their body in the position found, keep talking to and reassuring them, and call emergency medical services, move them only if: they are in immediate danger (e.g. a burning car), their airway is compromised (vomiting or fluid in the mouth), or CPR is needed and they are face down, when a move to perform CPR or clear the airway is unavoidable, use a log roll: several people turn the body over in one single motion, one person dedicated to supporting and aligning the head with the body, with the person at the head directing the roll
- **Important concepts:** the spinal cord's location of damage determining the extent of paralysis — lower-spine damage affecting leg use, higher damage risking loss of control over "vital life support systems such as my breathing system", spinal cord damage described as unable to be repaired, which the source gives as the reason for treating any suspicion of spinal injury as the most serious possibility rather than waiting for confirmation

procedures: for a bee sting (stinger left behind): scrape it out sideways with a flat edge (a credit or business card), never with tweezers or by squeezing at the top — both of those actions push more venom from the embedded sac into the wound

for a wasp sting (no stinger left behind) or a general insect bite: wash with soap and water, apply a cold compress, elevate the area to reduce swelling, and avoid scratching (which risks infection); avoid home remedies like vinegar or bicarbonate of soda, which the source states are "unlikely to help"

sections.body:
**Bee and wasp stings require different first-aid technique because only a bee leaves its stinger
embedded — a bee sting must be scraped out sideways with a flat edge, never squeezed or pulled with
tweezers, both of which push more venom into the wound — while general insect bites are treated
with wash, cold compress, and elevation, and every sting or bite should be watched for signs of
anaphylaxis.** `[02:01]` "With a bee sting, we can remove that quite easily by using a credit card
or a business card and we scrape it away. We don't use tweezers, because if we use tweezers... we
can inject any poison that's still left in that sting into the casualty."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:00]`–`[02:01]` The source frames this as a common point of confusion: "the reason I know it's
a bee that stung her and not a wasp is because there's a sting still left inside... wasps, although
they sting you, do not leave the sting behind, whereas bees do." This single anatomical fact is
what determines whether scraping-removal technique is needed at all.
sections.heading: Bee vs. wasp: the mechanical difference driving different treatment

sections.body:

and spreads quickly is more likely due to an allergy than to an infection,"** whereas infection
develops more gradually with pus, worsening pain, or systemic signs like fever and swollen glands.
Anaphylaxis-specific signs needing an emergency call are listed directly: wheezing, breathing
difficulty, facial swelling, nausea/vomiting, increased heart rate, dizziness, or faintness.

sections.body:

insect bite: itchy red lumps or swelling appearing immediately and lasting up to two hours, often
followed by a firmer itchy lump developing up to 24 hours later and lasting several days. Infection
signs: redness, tenderness, pus, spreading over several days. Anaphylaxis signs as listed above.

concepts: spinal cord damage described as unable to be repaired, which the source gives as the reason for treating any suspicion of spinal injury as the most serious possibility rather than waiting for confirmation

the spinal cord's location of damage determining the extent of paralysis — lower-spine damage affecting leg use, higher damage risking loss of control over "vital life support systems such as my breathing system"
emergencies: a suspected spinal injury (from a low-level fall, a road accident, a fall from height, or compression such as someone jumping on the back)
procedures: do not move a person with a suspected spinal injury; support their head and neck, keep them as still as possible, leave their body in the position found, keep talking to and reassuring them, and call emergency medical services
move them only if: they are in immediate danger (e.g. a burning car), their airway is compromised (vomiting or fluid in the mouth), or CPR is needed and they are face down

when a move to perform CPR or clear the airway is unavoidable, use a log roll: several people turn the body over in one single motion, one person dedicated to supporting and aligning the head with the body, with the person at the head directing the roll

sections.body:
**The core rule for a suspected spinal injury is not to move the person and to support their head
— "there's always going to be a possibility they might have a spine injury, so we always want to
keep them as still as possible" — with moving them justified only by immediate danger, a
compromised airway, or the need to perform CPR.** `[01:00]` "The simple rule to remember if a
spinal injury... is if you suspect someone's hurt their back, tell them to keep still, do not move
them."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]` The stated reasoning ties directly to anatomy: "our spinal cord is where the brain sends
signals to the rest of the body, and if that spinal cord becomes damaged it just can't be
repaired." The location of damage determines its severity — lower-spine damage is described as
risking loss of leg function, while higher damage "can result in a loss of control to my vital
life support systems such as my breathing system." Treating every suspected case as potentially
serious, rather than waiting to find out, follows directly from this "can't be repaired" framing.
sections.heading: Why: what spinal cord damage actually does

sections.body:
`[02:01]`–`[03:01]` When movement truly can't be avoided — turning someone face-down to perform
CPR, or because they're vomiting — the source specifies a **log roll**: the patient is turned "in a
single motion," requiring several people, with one person dedicated to supporting the head and
keeping it aligned with the body throughout. The person at the head is described as directing the
roll, which the source frames as requiring "good communication skills" among the helpers.
sections.heading: The log roll: the one sanctioned way to move someone

the key distinction driving the different CPR sequence: a drowning collapse is treated as a respiratory problem (lack of oxygen) rather than a cardiac one, similar in mechanism to why an infant or child might stop breathing, whereas a collapse on dry land is treated as more likely cardiac
emergencies: an unconscious adult recovered from water, not breathing
dry drowning — a child inhales water that triggers a vocal-cord spasm, preventing air from entering the lungs, without water actually entering the lungs
secondary/delayed drowning — inhaled water causes lung inflammation that can present hours to days (up to 72 hours) after the initial water exposure
procedures: if alone and the person hasn't recovered after one minute of CPR, leave to call emergency services, then resume care — this differs from an on-land collapse, where the ambulance is called immediately, before starting CPR
if breathing resumes, place in the recovery position and keep warm
if not breathing: open the airway, pinch the nose, and give 5 rescue breaths first (this may be enough on its own) — if not, begin 30 compressions to 2 breaths and continue for one minute
once the person is on dry land, open the airway and check breathing for 10 seconds as usual
only enter water to help if it's safe to do so; shout for help first
seek medical help immediately for any suspected dry or secondary drowning, even if the person seems to recover initially

sections.body:
**Because a drowning collapse is treated as a respiratory event rather than a cardiac one, the
CPR sequence differs from an on-land collapse: give 5 rescue breaths first, then 30 compressions to
2 breaths for a full minute, before leaving to call emergency services if alone — the reverse
priority from a dry-land collapse, where the ambulance is called immediately, before starting
CPR.** `[01:01]` "In drowning cases if the patient is not breathing then you would open the airway
and you'll pinch your nose and you'll deliver five rescue breaths... if not, then you would start
with 30 compressions followed by two breaths, and you continue doing that for one minute."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[02:01]` The source explains the underlying logic: "the patient has most likely stopped
breathing because of a lack of oxygen, a respiratory issue, not a cardiac issue... it's very, very
similar to the reason why a child or baby would have stopped breathing." Because rescue breaths
alone may restart breathing in a purely respiratory event, the source states one minute of CPR is
attempted before a lone rescuer leaves to call for help — contrasted directly with a dry-land
collapse, "as soon as you know they're not breathing you must call the ambulance straight away."
sections.heading: Why the sequence is reversed for drowning

sections.body:
`[03:03]` **Dry drowning**: water is inhaled through the nose or mouth and triggers "a spasm in the
airway," specifically of the vocal cords, which don't relax — water never actually reaches the
lungs, but the spasm itself blocks breathing. **Secondary/delayed drowning**: water is inhaled into
the lungs and causes inflammation or swelling of the small air sacs, which can develop "hours or
even days later... up to 72 hours afterward," preventing oxygen from reaching the bloodstream.
sections.heading: Dry drowning vs. secondary/delayed drowning

sections.body:
For dry or secondary drowning: difficulty breathing, a persistent cough, choking, sudden lethargy
or sleepiness, irritability, or vomiting, appearing at any point after a water incident, including
well after the person has left the water.

- **Dry drowning** — a vocal-cord spasm following water inhalation that blocks breathing without
  water ever entering the lungs. `[03:03]`
- **Secondary (delayed) drowning** — lung inflammation from inhaled water that can present up to
  72 hours after the initial exposure. `[03:03]`

sections.body:
**Heat exhaustion (body temperature 38°C and above — hot, sweaty, distressed) is managed with
shade, water, and calm; heat stroke (around 40°C, where the "thermostat" has failed and sweating
has stopped) is a medical emergency requiring immediate cooling — whole-body cold-water immersion
preferred, then a cold shower/hose, then ice packs at the neck/armpits/groin — while emergency
services are called.** `[02:01]` "Heat stroke... this is where the body's thermostat fails due to
the extreme temperature. The most obvious sign of heat stroke is they're no longer sweating, the
skin actually becomes dry."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:01]` The source gives a specific fallback order for cooling a heat stroke patient while
waiting for help: whole-body immersion from the neck down in water between 1 and 26°C is preferred;
if unavailable, a cold shower or garden hose; if that's also unavailable, large bags of ice wrapped
in a towel placed at the neck, armpits, and groin, or wet towels — with the caveat to swap a wet
towel for a dry one once the patient has cooled, to avoid then overcooling them.
sections.heading: The cooling-method priority order

emergency: "approximately three in every 100 children have at least one convulsion in their
lifetime" due to fever, because "a child's brain is not fully developed." A febrile convulsion can
also follow an injection or illness-driven temperature rise, not only outdoor heat exposure. Stated
treatment is identical to any seizure — protect, don't restrain — while also working to lower the
child's temperature, with escalation to emergency services "if ever you're in doubt."
sections.heading: Febrile convulsions: a heat-related complication in children

sections.body:
Heat exhaustion: hot, sweaty skin, increased breathing rate, distress. Heat stroke: dry skin (no
longer sweating) as the key escalation sign. Febrile convulsion: seizure-like convulsion in a
child, usually lasting under a minute but potentially up to five, that can look like — but the
source distinguishes from — an epileptic seizure.

sections.body:
**Most snake bites are treated by staying calm, keeping the bitten limb still, and getting to
hospital fast — with a long list of things NOT to do (no ice, no tourniquet, no cutting or
sucking, no commercial snake-bite kit) — while a pressure-immobilization bandage is reserved
strictly for a known bite from a neurotoxic/elapid snake, and is never a substitute for or
equivalent to a tourniquet.** `[05:07]` "No first aid is often less harmful than bad first aid,
especially when it comes to snake bites."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[04:07]`–`[05:07]` The source explains the mechanism behind each prohibited action: ice
"constrict[s]" small blood vessels, which "can produce dramatic tissue damage faster"; a
tourniquet keeps venom "concentrated near the bite," which "rapidly destroy[s] cells," whereas
allowing venom to spread and dilute "will... likely reduce the tissue damage"; aspirin or
ibuprofen "can make the bleeding a lot worse." Chasing, catching, or killing the snake risks "two
bites... to deal with."

procedures: breath-control technique: breathe in slowly for a count of four, hold for a count of four, breathe out slowly for a count of four, repeating until calm — with an occasional normal breath inserted if needed to avoid dizziness from too many deep breaths in a row
find a quiet place to sit, release tension in the shoulders and upper body, sit with a straight back, and loosen tight clothing before starting a breathing technique

re-breathing technique: cup both hands over the nose and mouth, breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth into the cupped hands, repeated no more than four times, to re-inhale some of the carbon dioxide just exhaled

seek emergency medical advice if unsure whether the presentation is hyperventilation or something else (e.g. a heart attack), since symptoms like chest pain can overlap — never leave the person alone in that uncertainty
{'other tips mentioned': 'humming, whistling, or singing can help regulate breathing'}

sections.body:
**Hyperventilation is over-breathing that depletes the body's carbon dioxide, producing symptoms
that drive further over-breathing in a self-reinforcing cycle — broken by either a slow
paced-breathing technique (in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4) or a cupped-hands re-breathing
technique, not by the older brown-paper-bag method, which the source says isn't taught anymore.**
`[01:00]` "These reactions are literally caused by having too little carbon dioxide, and they're
very frightening in themselves and they can lead to more over-breathing, and this is known as the
vicious circle of hyperventilation."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:01]`–`[04:04]` The **breath-control technique**: sit somewhere quiet, release tension, breathe
in for a count of four, hold for four, out for four, repeating until calm. The **re-breathing
technique**: cup both hands over the nose and mouth and breathe in through the nose, out through
the mouth, into the cupped hands — no more than four repetitions — to re-inhale some of the just-
exhaled, CO2-rich air. The source addresses the brown paper bag directly: it works on the same
principle, but **"medical research on using it to help hyperventilation is divided on why that
really actually works... in first aid we don't actually teach that method anymore"** — partly
because holding a bag over someone's face can itself be frightening, and it must never be a plastic
bag.
sections.heading: Two techniques, and why the paper bag isn't one of them

sections.body:
`[05:06]` A specific safety caveat: hyperventilation and a heart attack can both present with chest
pain, so **"if you've ever seen about someone... hyperventilating and you're not quite sure if it
is there, or maybe it is a heart attack that's causing it... always seek emergency medical advice,
never just leave this person."**
sections.heading: Distinguishing from a more serious condition

Difficulty catching breath, chest tightness, rapid pulse, sweating/clamminess, tingling or numbness
(especially in the extremities), vision problems, rigid muscles and cramps, sudden emotional
outbursts (crying), and feeling too hot or too cold.

**Anaphylaxis is treated as a medical emergency requiring an immediate call to emergency services
and use of the person's own adrenaline auto-injector pen, pressed against the outer thigh through
clothing and held for a consistent 10 seconds regardless of which pen brand is used.** `[02:02]`
"If you suspect that you or someone else has experienced symptoms of anaphylactic reaction, you
must call the emergency medical services instantly, then you're going to get their auto injector
pen for them to use."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:02]`–`[04:02]` The cap is described as commonly misunderstood: "the cap is not where the
needle comes from... the cap releases the needle from the opposite end of the pen." The injector is
pushed against the patient's leg until it clicks and held for a count that differs by brand — the
EpiPen's official hold time is 3 seconds, Jext's is 10 — with the source's explicit simplification:
**"I'd always encourage you to hold them for 10 seconds... it saves any confusion."** The pen
cannot be reused after one dose.
sections.heading: Auto-injector technique, step by step

sections.body:
`[03:02]`–`[04:02]` The source gives three specific reasons a person with severe allergies should
always carry two pens: the first injection may have missed or been interrupted if the person
moved, the helper may have accidentally injected themselves instead, or the single dose inside one
pen may not be enough while waiting for an ambulance that "can take a while to get there." A second
dose is administered after 5 minutes specifically if the person resumes struggling to breathe.
sections.heading: Why two pens, and when a second dose is warranted

sections.body:
General allergic reaction: sneezing, wheezing, coughing, skin rash — varying by how the allergen
was encountered (e.g. airway symptoms from an inhaled allergen like pollen). Anaphylaxis: itchy
skin or raised red rash, swollen eyes/lips/hands/feet, lightheadedness or faintness, wheezy/narrowed
airway, breathing difficulty, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, collapse, and unconsciousness.

sections.body:
**A stroke is recognized using the FAST mnemonic (Face, Arms, Speech, Time), and the moment any of
those signs appear, the stated rule is to call emergency services immediately — the source
explicitly frames faster identification as directly improving how much of the brain can be saved
and the person's chance of recovery.** `[04:01]` "A good way of remembering this is a mnemonic FAST,
which stands for face, arms, speech, time... the more quickly you identify that someone is having a
stroke, then the sooner they're going to receive medical treatment, which means that more of the
brain can be saved."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:00]`–`[03:01]` The source names two main stroke types: a **clot** blocking an artery to the
brain (via thrombosis forming in the artery, an embolism carried from elsewhere in the body, or a
blockage in small deep brain vessels), and a **bleed/hemorrhage** from a burst blood vessel in or
around the brain. A **TIA** ("transient ischemic attack," or "mini stroke") is a temporary version
of the same blockage, with symptoms that resolve — but the source is explicit this is still a
medical emergency: "there is a risk of more serious strokes in the future... you must always seek
emergency medical treatment if this happens immediately."

emergency medical services, because the sooner you get that person help, the better chance they
have of recovery."**

is treated by getting the casualty into a chest-opening position, using their own reliever
inhaler — ideally through a spacer for a more precise dose — one puff at a time, escalating to
emergency services if there's no improvement after five minutes.** `[03:02]` "With the inhaler
without the spacer, we're going to encourage them to push down on it and breathe in and take one
puff every minute. After five minutes, if they're not feeling better, then we're going to call the
emergency medical services."

problem breathing out," since narrowed, inflamed airways trap air on exhale. Stated severity

them children), and around 2,000 people die of asthma per year in the UK — used to argue that a
common condition still deserves to be "treated seriously."

and night; reliever inhalers (typically blue, often containing salbutamol) are for an active
attack. The source is explicit an asthma sufferer having an attack should use only their own
inhaler, for two reasons: cross-contamination between people's inhalers, and the possibility the
medication inside differs from person to person.
