frostbite — deeper tissue/muscle/blood-vessel freezing, more serious
hypothermia — from cold air exposure or cold-water immersion
procedures: for frost nip: warm the affected area gently yourself (e.g. tucking cold fingertips under the armpits), watching that it doesn't progress to frostbite

for frostbite: do not rub or massage the area (this worsens it); rewarm only slowly, using water no warmer than 40°C, and seek emergency medical guidance since the rewarming process is usually very painful

for hypothermia: do not reheat quickly — rapid rewarming can complicate the condition and cause cardiac arrest; if the person is wet, remove wet clothing (water draws heat out 20-25 times faster than air) and dry them by patting gently, then warm gradually

prevention: carry a change of clothes, towels, and blankets whenever wet conditions or cold water are a possibility, even in summer, and note a standard foil blanket alone is not sufficient to warm someone up, only to help maintain warmth

cardiac arrest — with wet clothing removed immediately since water draws heat from the body far
faster than air.** `[00:00]` "It's really important actually not to reheat them too quickly, as
this can complicate the matters and it can actually cause a cardiac arrest."

warming the area (e.g. tucking fingertips under the armpits) — with a caution to watch that it
doesn't progress further. **Frostbite**: described as more serious, where "the body's tissues,
muscles, and blood vessels freeze." Its rewarming rule is stricter and the opposite instinct from
what might seem intuitive: **"never rub or massage frostbitten areas because that's going to make
it worse"**, and rewarming should use water no warmer than 40°C, done slowly, with emergency medical
guidance since the process "is usually quite painful."

governed by specific triggers (unknown history, over five minutes, repeated seizures without

sections.body:
`[00:00]` A seizure is described as "a sudden burst of excess electric activity in our brains
causing a temporary disruption in the normal messages passing between our brain cells." The source
is explicit that presentation varies by where in the brain the activity starts and how it spreads:
**"never think there's a normal seizure."** Named causes include head injury, hypo/hyperglycemia in
diabetics, drug or alcohol withdrawal, and — specifically in young children — fever-driven febrile
convulsions.
sections.heading: What a seizure is, and why "there's not a normal seizure"

sections.body:
`[01:00]`–`[02:00]` The tonic-clonic seizure is presented as the most common generalized type, in
two phases: the **tonic stage** (body goes rigid from strong muscle contraction, consciousness is
lost, the person falls), followed by the **clonic stage** (muscles repeatedly contract and relax,
producing visible shaking) lasting seconds to minutes. Afterward, the person "gradually regain[s]
consciousness but may still be confused" for a variable period, possibly with soreness, headache,
and a need to sleep.
sections.heading: The tonic-clonic pattern, as one example among many

sections.body:
Sudden loss of consciousness, a rigid arched-back body, noisy or difficult breathing, convulsions,
possible loss of bladder control, and post-seizure confusion or deep sleep. A possible pre-seizure
warning symptom is described — odd movements, clothing worn oddly, unusual smells, or a metallic
taste — flagged as inconsistent: "not everybody has these... most seizures commonly occur without
any warning whatsoever." (The caption transcribes the name for this as "orders," which is almost
certainly a mishearing of the clinical term "auras" — see the note on this in Glossary terms.)

sections.body:

  consciousness and falling. `[01:00]`
- **Clonic stage** — the convulsive phase following the tonic stage, where muscles repeatedly
  contract and relax. `[02:00]`
- **Febrile convulsion** — a seizure in a young child caused by a rapid rise in body temperature

- No new named clinical term is confidently introduced here: the source's caption reads "orders"
  for what is described as a pre-seizure warning symptom (odd movement, unusual smell or taste)

**Scene safety comes before treating an electrocution victim — the person may still be "live" and
dangerous to touch, so the first step is always to eliminate the electrical hazard (cutting power
for low voltage, staying far back and calling for help for high voltage) before approaching at
all.** `[02:03]` "Always be aware that the patient may be live if they're still in contact with the
electrical supply... if there's any doubt at all, do not touch them. Always make sure the power is
off."

`[01:02]` The source explains the underlying mechanism: when a body part contacts or nears a live
source, "the body becomes the link from live to earth, and the electricity transfers through the
body to earth," causing muscles to convulse. A current as small as **10 milliamps** can cause
muscle contraction strong enough that "a hand... can close around the source... and cannot release
it" — meaning a victim may be unable to let go even if conscious. In wet conditions, a current of
just **60 milliamps** "can be fatal," since moisture "reduces the body's resistance" and can disrupt
the heart's electrical activity, causing cardiac arrest.

concepts: the shared mechanism behind two counter-intuitive instructions: both urinating on a jellyfish sting and rinsing it with fresh water are stated to activate unfired stingers and release additional venom, rather than providing relief
emergencies: a jellyfish sting, ranging from a painful mark to (rarely) a severe, life-threatening reaction
a weever fish sting, from standing on one buried in sand
procedures: do not urinate on a jellyfish sting — explicitly stated to potentially worsen it, the same way fresh water does, by releasing more venom from unfired stingers

for a jellyfish sting: remove any stuck tentacles with a flat object (e.g. a credit card), never fingers, and without rubbing (which can trigger more venom release); rinse with seawater, not fresh water; then soak the area in water as hot as tolerable for at least 30 minutes (or use hot flannels/towels if soaking isn't possible)
for a weever fish sting: remove the embedded dorsal-fin spines from the foot, then immerse the foot in water at 40°C (104°F) or higher for at least 30 minutes
seek medical help or a lifeguard immediately if uncomfortable performing self-treatment, or if in doubt about any marine sting or bite
wear shoes on rocks and walk slowly into the water to avoid cuts from barnacles/shells and crab pinches

sections.body:
**Two specific pieces of "common knowledge" about jellyfish stings are directly corrected: fresh
water and urine both risk releasing more venom from unfired stingers rather than helping — the
correct sequence is removing tentacles with a flat object, rinsing with seawater, then soaking in
water as hot as tolerable for at least 30 minutes.** `[02:02]` "Despite the folklore, urinating on a
jellyfish sting may actually cause the stingers to release more venom rather than actually
providing relief... please do not wee over any wound."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[02:02]` Tentacle removal: "use a flat object such as a credit card... do not use your
fingers... do not rub them either... you can aggravate them, which will set off the poison." The
source gives the same underlying mechanism for both myths it corrects: "fresh water actually
activates the stingers that have not yet released the venom," and urine works the same way,
"despite the folklore." After removal and seawater rinsing, the treatment is heat: "soak the area
in very warm water, as hot as you can possibly tolerate it, for at least 30 minutes."
sections.heading: Jellyfish: removal technique and the fresh-water/urine myth

sections.body:
`[02:02]`–`[03:02]` Weever fish "bury themselves in the sand" and sting via a dorsal fin embedding
in the foot when stepped on, "which causes excruciating pain." Treatment: remove the embedded
spines, then immerse the foot in water at "40 degrees Celsius or higher... for no less than 30
minutes." The source explicitly permits deferring to a lifeguard or medical professional instead of
self-treating: "if you do not feel comfortable performing first aid on yourself, please make sure
you seek medical advice immediately."
sections.heading: Weever fish: a hidden, high-pain hazard

sections.body:
Jellyfish sting: a painful, red, irritated mark in most cases, rarely progressing to a severe or
life-threatening reaction. Weever fish sting: excruciating localized foot pain from venom injected
via the dorsal fin spines. General coastal hazards: cuts from barnacles/shells, crab pinches.

concepts: dehydration named as a serious complication of food poisoning, especially for the young, the elderly, or in a hot climate
poison/toxin defined broadly — not only swallowed, but absorbed through skin or eyes, inhaled, or injected, then carried through the bloodstream to organs and tissue
prevention framed as the primary defense against plant/fungi poisoning — knowing what plants are in one's own garden or house and removing ones dangerous to children or pets
emergencies: food poisoning (bacterial or viral contamination, e.g. salmonella or E. coli)
plant or fungi poisoning (e.g. foxglove, poisonous berries, death cap mushroom)
swallowed poison (household chemicals, drugs — legal or illegal)
procedures: do not induce vomiting in a conscious casualty, since vomiting can cause further damage as the substance passes back through the respiratory tract, mouth, and nose
for food poisoning: rest, hydration (rehydration powders or isotonic drinks), and seeking medical help if needed; report to authorities/employer if relevant (e.g. a shared food source)
for plant/fungi poisoning: try to identify the plant or fungus (photograph or bring a sample) to help medical treatment
identify what was taken, how much, and when; reassure the casualty and call emergency medical services with as much detail as possible to help hospital treatment

if the casualty becomes unconscious, open the airway, check breathing, and begin CPR if needed — using a face shield or covering the mouth and blowing through the nose to avoid cross-contamination from residual chemical
stay calm and non-accusatory, since a scared casualty (especially a child) may not disclose what or how much they took

sections.body:
**Across all forms of poisoning covered — swallowed chemicals or drugs, food poisoning, and
plant/fungi poisoning — the shared first-aid response is to identify the substance, stay calm,
avoid inducing vomiting, and call emergency medical services with as much detail as possible.**
`[01:00]` "The treatment firstly is to identify what has actually been taken... how many have they
swallowed, what they swallowed, and try and reassure them and call the emergency medical
services... this information will assist doctors to give the appropriate treatment."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:02]` The source is explicit that inducing vomiting in a conscious poisoning casualty is
wrong: "vomiting can cause more damage and the chemical... can actually cover the whole of the
respiratory tract, mouth, and also inside the nose, causing more of respiratory issues." If the
casualty stops breathing, the source adds a self-protection step not mentioned in this
collection's other CPR notes: use a face shield, or cover the casualty's mouth and breathe through
their nose instead, to avoid the rescuer's own mouth contacting residual chemical.
sections.heading: Why not to induce vomiting, and how to protect yourself during rescue breaths

sections.body:
`[03:02]`–`[04:03]` Food poisoning is attributed to bacteria or viruses in contaminated food or
drink, commonly salmonella or E. coli found in meats in the UK, with onset from hours up to a day
after eating. The named serious complication is dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea, "especially
serious for the young and also the old, or if you're living in a hot climate." Treatment is rest,
hydration (naming rehydration powders and isotonic drinks), and seeking medical help if needed —
plus notifying others who may have shared the same food source.
sections.heading: Food poisoning and dehydration

sections.body:
`[05:05]`–`[06:05]` Named examples: the foxglove plant (also called "Dead Man's Bells," "dog's
fingers," "fairy fingers"), whose toxins "directly affect the heart muscles" and can slow the
heartbeat or cause a heart attack; poisonous berries; and the death cap mushroom, which "causes
severe watery diarrhea between 6 to 12 hours after ingestion... and it can be fatal." The source
frames prevention (knowing what's growing in one's own garden) as the primary defense, since
diagnosis and treatment depend on identifying the exact plant or fungus involved.
sections.heading: Plant and fungi poisoning

sections.body:
Swallowed poison: vomiting (sometimes blood-stained), nausea, diarrhea, impaired consciousness,
pain or burning, and visible empty containers as a scene clue. Food poisoning: nausea, cramping,
abdominal pain, blood-stained diarrhea, headache, fever, shock, impaired consciousness. Plant/fungi
poisoning: nausea, diarrhea, and — for certain mushrooms — hallucinations.
